newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: WAGES INCREASES WON'T AFFECT INFLATION
The centre for Industrial Relations Research says there'll be wage increases of more than six per cent next year which won't affect inflation.
The government and employer groups have criticised rises in the metals and construction industry recently, arguing they threaten a wages breakout.
The Centre's Ron Callus says rises of above six per cent will be delivered in those and other industries in the New Year, which will be rewards for better workplace productivity.
HOME LOANS GETTING MORE AFFORDABLE
A combination of lower interest rates and slightly higher wages is making home loans in Australia more affordable.
The Citibank-Real Estate Institute survey shows loans have become more affordable in all States and Territories in the September quarter.
Citibank chief economist Stephen Koukoulas says it's good news for home buyers.
CHANGES TO INDIGENOUS HERITAGE LAWS
The Federal Government has announced details of the substantial changes it plans to make to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Heritage Protection Act.
Aboriginal Affairs Minister, John Herron, says the changes would mean the Federal legislation would become a last resort.
It would only apply where State and Territory laws fail to meet minimum standards or where there are considerations of national interest.
Senator Herron says the Government is aware of the importance of heritage protection to indigenous people and will ensure that culture and beliefs are properly protected.
But he says the Hindmarsh Island Bridge case has been a gross waste of money and has undermined public confidence in Governments' ability to deal sensibly with indigenous heritage isues.
EUTHANASIA SUPPORT FUND
Pro-euthanasia advocate Dr Phillip Nitschke says Australians are prepared to dig into their wallets to fight for the right to die.
A fund has been established to fight attempts to overturn the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law.
Dr Nitschke says the plight of terminally ill South Australian woman Janet Mills who wants to die, has attracted widespread public sympathy and monetary donations.
He says there's overwhelming opposition to the Kevin Andrews private members bill which seeks to overturn the Territory law.
HANSON CALLS FOR INQUIRY INTO ALL MP'S SPENDING
Independent MP Pauline Hanson says she used her electoral allowance to pay for a new TV because she monitors more television news outside office hours.

Federal Administrative Services Minister, David Jull, will write to Ms Hanson, asking her to explain why she spent part of her electoral allowance on a new television for her home, and put her old set in the electorate office.
Ms Hanson says with the media scrutiny she's under, she has to be meticulous in her accounting.
She's called for an inquiry into all Federal MP's spending. But Mr Jull's office says electoral allowances are set by the remuneration tribunal.
MINISTER REJECTS MEDIA MAGNATE'S CRITICISM
Federal Communications Minister, Richard Alston, has rejected criticisms of Government media policy by Canadian media proprietor, Conrad Black.
Mr Black is selling his company's stake in the Fairfax newspaper group to New Zealand group, Brierley Investements.
The Canadian says existing foreign ownership rules were creating an extremely difficult environment.
But the Minister says, as far as he's aware, Mr Black never formally or informally approached the Government to increase his stake in Fairfax.
Senator Alston says the decision to sell was a commercial one.
KENNETT TO INVESTIGATE RACIAL ABUSE COMPLAINTS
Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, says he'll investigate complaints Malaysian students studying in Victoria have been subject to racial abuse.
Malaysia's Prime Minister, Dr Mahathir Mohamad, has threatened to recall Malaysian students from Australia if they're safety is threatened.
Mr Kennett has urged any student with a complaint to tell authorities.
